title: Two federal programs helped expand police funding by over 200%
主要内容: Two federal programs, the Community Oriented Policing Services (COPS) and Byrne Justice Assistance Grants (Byrne JAG), have significantly expanded police funding in the United States. Between 1982 and 2015, federal spending on policing grew by 354%, outpacing both local and state spending. In 2015, local governments accounted for over two-thirds of police spending, while the federal government contributed 20.4%. The COPS program, established in 1994 under President Bill Clinton, provided $304 million in 2019 to law enforcement agencies. Byrne JAG, created in 1988 and consolidated in 2005, still averages around $435 million annually. Despite these increases, debates persist about the effectiveness of federal funding for law enforcement. Two federal programs helped expand police funding by over 200%. Some studies even suggested that the grants might not have been effective in cities with more than 250,000 people. In 2006, the Bush administration sought to eliminate all Byrne JAG funding due to a lack of demonstrable results, but it was eventually reauthorized through 2012. The movement to defund the police stems from the same question on whether communities benefit from millions of dollars in funding from federal, state and local governments. "People are recognizing that budgets often are related to power," says Rashawn Ray, a governance studies fellow at the Brookings Institution. "And in law enforcement, one of the things that we see is that the larger their budgets get, that hasn't necessarily correlated with a reduction in crime. So then people start saying, then why do their budgets look the way that it does?" Only time and more research will determine whether defunding the police will create safer communities. One thing that is for sure, the movement is leading to critical conversations at the local level on how to best protect citizens. "I think that this whole notion of defunding the police is an important conversation that's happening," said Ashton. "I think that we really need to think as a country about where we're investing in local, state and federal dollars, and how we're making the most use of that money to positively impact communities."
